title: Arrest warrant issued vs Sara Duterte over grave threats
author: Isabelle Pechay
article_text: MANILA, Philippines — Branch 98 of the Quezon City Regional Trial Court has issued a warrant of arrest against Vice President Sara Duterte over three counts of grave threats, her lawyer said Friday. “Today, the Quezon City RTC has issued a warrant of arrest against the vice president,” lawyer Paul Lawrence Lim said in a statement. “Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies ,” Lim added. Lim is Duterte’s counsel in the grave threats charges filed by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI). In a contributed photo of the arrest warrant against Duterte dated Sept. 4, the court set bail at P120,000 for each of the three counts of grave threats. The Inquirer asked Duterte’s camp whether she would post bail but had yet to receive a substantive response as of posting time. Lim said he would get back to the Inquirer on the matter. The NBI case stemmed from Duterte’s remarks during an online press briefing on Nov. 23, 2024, in which she said she had spoken to someone and instructed that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., first lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez be killed if she were killed. “Do not worry about my security because I already spoke to someone. I said, ‘If I am killed, kill BBM, Liza Araneta, and Martin Romualdez.’ No joke, no joke,” Duterte said. READ: DOJ files grave threat case vs VP Sara Duterte Duterte is also facing an impeachment trial before the Senate, where she is accused of several offenses outlined in the Articles of Impeachment. title: Malacañang orders alternative learning modes amid rains, haze
author: Luisa Cabato
article_text: MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang has ordered alternative learning modes at all levels in public and private educational institutions in the National Capital Region (NCR) and several provinces on Friday, Sept. 4, in view of the anticipated continued heavy rainfall associated with the enhanced southwest monsoon and the poor air quality currently being experienced in the NCR. The unhealthy air quality was caused by the haze from the severe forest and peatland fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra, Indonesia. Also included in the order are the following areas: READ: Public urged to take precautions amid Metro Manila haze Memorandum Circular No. 134 said this alternative mode of learning shall be implemented unless the respective local chief executives direct the cancellation or suspension of classes. “Further thereto, the localized cancellation or suspension of classes in other areas may be implemented by their respective Local Chief Executives, pursuant to relevant laws, rules, and regulations,” it read. /das By providing an email address. title: NBI files qualified human trafficking raps vs Leviste, 6 others
author: Mary Joy Salcedo
article_text: MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has filed qualified human trafficking complaints before the Department of Justice (DOJ) against Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste, former Negros Oriental Rep. Jacinto “Jing” Paras, and five others following its investigation into the alleged “honey trap” plot targeting Executive Secretary Ralph Recto. “Kumpleto, nandirito na yung mga ebidensya, all the attachments, and we are filing a violation of the anti-human trafficking law. So qualified human trafficking ang ipa-file natin to seven individuals,” NBI Director Melvin Matibag said in an ambush interview on Friday. (It’s complete; the evidence is here, all the attachments, and we are filing a violation of the anti-human trafficking law. So, qualified human trafficking is what we are going to file against seven individuals.) Qualified human trafficking is nonbailable. READ: Talent manager details alleged ‘honey trap’ plot vs Recto Aside from Leviste and Paras, the NBI also filed the same charges against talent manager Alias Ken and the four lawyers from the Rondain and Mendiola Law Firm who are supposedly tasked to create fabricated statements against Recto. The four lawyers are Ruy Rondain, Orlando Mendiola, Patrick Criaga, and Josemilio Manuel Apostol. READ: NBI considers ethics complaint vs. Leviste after trafficking raps The NBI’s National Capital Region, led by regional director Emeterio Dongallo Jr., arrived at the DOJ headquarters in Ermita, Manila, this Friday afternoon to file the charges. Dongallo told the INQUIRER in a Viber message that the charges were officially lodged around 3 p.m. Matibag also said the bureau is considering filing an ethics complaint against Leviste at the House of Representatives and a disbarment case against the four lawyers next week. “Nag-iimbento ng kalokohan gamit ang buwis habang lubog ang bayan. Nakakaawa ang nangyayari sa ating bansa,” Leviste said. (They’re inventing nonsense using taxes while the country is drenched in floods. What’s happening in our country is pathetic.) Paras, meanwhile, said in a phone interview with the INQUIRER that he is ready to face the complaints since these were only “fabricated.” Mendiola, one of the four lawyers, said he may give a comment “after I have seen the criminal complaint.” Rondain, however, has yet to respond to the query. The investigation into the supposed “honey trap” operation began following the arrest of Alias Ken last July 28 over a human trafficking case. Ken earlier said he met Paras and the lawyers in a restaurant in July to supposedly plan the “character assassination” scheme in which four of his female artists would issue fabricated statements claiming that Recto forced them to use illegal drugs and have sex with him. The lawyers, who allegedly introduced themselves as Leviste’s representatives, were tasked with crafting the “script,” or fabricated statements targeting Recto, the talent manager said. Ken also claimed that Leviste was the financier of the supposed modus. By providing an email address. I agree to the Terms of Use and acknowledge that I have read the Privacy Policy .

title: Senators talk of revisiting impeachment trial’s 16-vote conviction threshold
author: Tina G. Santos
article_text: MANILA, Philippines — Senators have discussed the possibility of lowering the 16-vote conviction threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial due to the absence of four of their colleagues. Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri said on Thursday that the issue was raised during a caucus held the previous day. “There are some senators that have questioned the threshold and it may come up sooner or later,” Zubiri said in a press conference. “There are those who are detained, one is at large. So I think that’s the issue now.” READ: Escudero maintains: 16 votes needed to convict Sara Duterte He was referring to Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, both detained on plunder charges, and Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, a fugitive facing an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court. A fourth, Sen. Loren Legarda, is abroad on medical leave. Zubiri noted that the Senate “still had a complete state” when Sen. Francis “Chiz” Escudero, the impeachment court’s presiding officer, made the 16-vote ruling in July. “That issue has to be answered soon enough by the presiding officer,” he said. On July 6, the first day of Duterte’s impeachment trial, Escudero declared that conviction will still require at least 16 votes from senator-judges. He made the pronouncement in his opening statement where he tackled the threshold questions that will guide the conduct of the proceedings and rulings. “The Charter provides that the Senate shall be composed of 24 senators, without a tinge of doubt, two-thirds of the figure or not less than 16 members, is an unquestionable compliance with the requisite number of votes mentioned in Section 21 of Article 7,” said Escudero. “It behooves, therefore, all of us, to observe the same fidelity to the Constitution, in this trial, which affects not only the mere ratification of a treaty, but more so affects the substantial rights of the respondent, as well as the sovereign will of the people as expressed in the overwhelming mandate given to her,” he added. Escudero also said those who disagree with the threshold can seek judicial relief with the Supreme Court. While no one among the senator-judges challenged it then, questions over the conviction threshold have persisted as the number of senator-judges decreased over the course of the trial due to legal or medical reasons. READ: Ridon: Only impeachment court can decide Duterte trial vote threshold Zubiri said the best way to resolve the issue would be to debate it publicly. He added that should the Senate decide to change the threshold, it was expected that it would be challenged before the high court. In various interviews, lawyers Jay Tolosa and San Juan Rep. Ysabel Maria Zamora of the House prosecution panel, along with spokesperson and former Surigao del Norte Rep. Robert Ace Barbers, said the team was not entertaining the idea of pushing to lower the threshold. “Our position on this has been consistent from the very start. We don’t engage in vote counting. At the end of the day, our priority here is to establish an airtight case. We will ensure that, with our case, this will be backed by solid evidence,” Tolosa said. “So that when the trial ends, regardless of what will be the final interpretation of the two-thirds threshold, we will get these numbers. So that is the priority of the prosecution from the start, and it remains to be our priority until now,” he added. Former Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) president Domingo Cayosa, however, said earlier that the threshold may be lowered to reflect who among the 24 senator-judges were present to participate in the trial. Cayosa said this would be the “fair and practical” reading of the 1987 Constitution as it is in accordance with the spirit of the Charter, which is “not restrictive.” The operative concept, he added, that ties such an interpretation is the word “two-thirds of all members of the Senate.” “[Estrada, Dela Rosa, and Marcoleta] are all alive and are not yet unseated by any of the constitutionally allowed modes of removal, so they are still senators,” Cayosa said. “Except when they transform themselves into an impeachment court, they all become judges.” He pointed out that this is where the nuance in interpreting the constitutional provision comes in “because how can you be a judge when you were not there, [and] you did not observe and participate.” “But if one is on the side of the defense,” he added, a “simple and strictly literal” reading of the Charter would put the voting threshold at 16. Last month, Bicol Saro Rep. Terry Ridon said only the impeachment court can decide on the number of votes needed to convict Duterte. By providing an email address. title: Ombudsman orders BFP chief dismissed; graft, bribe raps filed
author: John Eric Mendoza
article_text: MANILA, Philippines — Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) chief Jesus Fernandez has been ordered dismissed by the Office of the Ombudsman following the filing of graft and bribery charges against him at the Sandiganbayan. The anti-graft body said the criminal cases against Fernandez and one private individual stemmed from the P14.7-million bribe that the official allegedly received in connection with the BFP’s procurement of 132 ambulances worth P485 million last year. “The Ombudsman found prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction to charge Fernandez,” it said in a statement. READ: Ex-BFP chief charged over P485-M ambulance deal The BFP official is facing charges for two counts of indirect bribery and two counts of violation of Section 3(b) of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act. In relation to a separate, administrative case that arose from the same transaction, the Ombudsman said it had found Fernandez guilty of grave misconduct and of conduct prejudicial to the best interest of the service. “This carries the penalty of dismissal from the service, including cancellation of eligibility, forfeiture of retirement benefits, and perpetual disqualification from reemployment in government service,” it said. There was no immediate reply from Fernandez when the Inquirer sought him for comment. According to the Ombudsman, the actions against Fernandez started with the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) launching a fact-finding investigation into the BFP’s procurement of 132 units of Type 1 Basic Life Support ambulances. The contract for the vehicles, the Ombudsman said, was awarded to Toyota Mabolo, which entered into a joint venture with Autozone Prime Distributors Inc. for the project. READ: Remulla: Over 200 BFP officers under probe for ‘slot-selling’ scheme The joint venture’s representative, Rosaverna Sangga, was also charged with two counts of Corruption of Public Officials under Article 212 of the Revised Penal Code. Investigators alleged that Fernandez received a total of P14.752 million as “SOP” — a code word for a bribe in government contracts — from Sangga. The money was allegedly delivered on two occasions, with Sangga handing over P10.752 million to Fernandez on Nov. 21, 2024, and another P4 million on Sept. 25, 2025. By providing an email address. title: DOJ: 15-yr-old suspect in school shooting ‘acted with discernment’
author: Kathleen de Villa
article_text: MANILA, Philippines — The older one of the two teenage suspects in the recent deadly school shooting incident in Tacloban City is facing additional criminal charges despite his young age, according to an official of the Department of Justice (DOJ). Justice Undersecretary Ian Norman Dato on Thursday said Tacloban City prosecutors had ordered the filing of frustrated murder and attempted murder charges against the 15-year-old boy who was determined to have “acted with discernment” when he brought a gun to the school and opened fire. The boy is one of the two Grade 9 students tagged as the shooters in the attack that killed three fellow students and wounded 20 others at San Jose National High School on June 22. READ: Tacloban prosecs to file criminal raps vs 15-yr-old boy over school shooting The upcoming filings against the 15-year-old are on top of the five cases—for three counts of murder and two counts of attempted murder—earlier filed against him on July 13 at the family court of the Tacloban Regional Trial Court. “Our prosecutors found that he acted with discernment and in conspiracy with a second minor,” Dato said in a press briefing. Under the amended Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act, a child between 15 and 18 years of age shall be exempted from criminal liability unless he or she acted with discernment based on the findings of the prosecutors during preliminary investigation. The other minor is aged 14 and considered exempt from criminal liability under the law. Both minors, classified in legal parlance as children in conflict with the law, have since been placed in a rehabilitation center of the Department of Social Welfare and Development. As to the new charges against the 15-year-old, the prosecutors recommended bail at P72,000 each for four counts of frustrated murder and P36,000 each for three counts of attempted murder, Dato said. Meanwhile, the aunt of the 14-year-old student, Police Staff Sergeant Arla Ray Paciencia, is facing charges for reckless imprudence resulting in multiple homicide and physical injuries, for allowing her government-issued 9mm Glock 17 pistol to be accessed by her nephew and used in the campus schooting. Paciencia, who has since been relieved of police duty, earlier told a Senate inquiry in July that her nephew broke into her house and stole her gun, which she said was kept in a “plastic locker.” /das By providing an email address. title: NBI confirms Chuangxing rebars used in collapsed Pampanga building
author: Isabelle Pechay
article_text: MANILA, Philippines — Steel bars recovered from the rubble of a collapsed building in Angeles City, Pampanga, were traced to a steel manufacturing plant under investigation, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) said Thursday. The disclosure was made during the Senate Committee on Economic Affairs’ second hearing on the domestic steel industry, where lawmakers continued to examine the possible use of substandard steel products in buildings and other structures. READ: Chinese owned plant in Pampanga linked to substandard steel bars Sen. Risa Hontiveros, who chairs the panel, asked whether the bureau could confirm that the steel bars recovered from the collapsed Pampanga building indeed came from Chuangxing Steel Inc. NBI Senior Agent, lawyer Zulikha Marie Conales confirmed the finding. “We confirm, we were able to recover rebars from the rubbles of the (collapsed) building in Pampanga, Madam Chair,” she said. The confirmation came amid ongoing investigation into allegations that Chuangxing, a Chinese-owned steel plant in Magalang, Pampanga, may have produced and distributed alleged substandard steel bars to different parts of the country and were later used in construction. Chuangxing was raided and shut down on July 18 after authorities discovered allegedly substandard steel products and radioactive materials inside the facility. The raid came weeks after the May 24 collapse of a nine-story building under construction in Barangay Balibago, which left 27 dead. READ: Owner, contractor of collapsed Pampanga building faces P11M in fines Hontiveros also asked Conales about reports that 70 percent of the defective steel used in a damaged building in Mindanao came from Sanjia, another steel manufacturing plant under scrutiny by authorities. “We confirm, madam chair,” Conales said, referring to the NBI’s investigation of the site. The NBI had earlier raided Sanjia’s 22.6-hectare plant at the Phividec Industrial Estate in Tagoloan, Misamis Oriental, where radioactive materials were found, prompting the temporary shutdown of the facility. Hontiveros said the NBI’s findings raised concerns about where else the alleged substandard steel may have been used. “Grabe po yun because then we need to think about saan pa napunta yung ibang ganoong klaseng substandard na products, saan pang ibang mga gusali dito sa ating bansa,” she said. title: UP study: Resort visitors willing to pay P75 to conserve Mt. Makiling
author: Cristina Eloisa Baclig
environment_keywords: environmental, natural resources, forest, forests, watershed, conservation, wildlife, ecosystems, recycling, water conservation
article_text: MANILA, Philippines — Visitors to resorts in Calamba City and Los Baños, Laguna, said they were willing to pay about P75 per visit for improved conservation of Mt. Makiling’s groundwater, a University of the Philippines Los Baños (UPLB) study found. If captured through a proposed water user fee, the amount could generate an estimated P159.52 million a year for groundwater conservation, resort water conservation measures and the management of Mt. Makiling, according to the study. The estimate was based on an online survey of 492 resort visitors, who were asked how much they would be willing to pay under a hypothetical program that required resorts to recycle and treat pool water and support groundwater conservation. The researchers used a contingent valuation method and interval regression to estimate the visitors’ willingness to pay. The study, “Potential Contribution of Tourism for Groundwater Conservation in Mt. Makiling, the Philippines,” was written by Margaret M. Calderon, Analyn L. Codilan, Jan Joseph V. Dida, Vanessa M. Palma-Torres, Angela Marie S. Alducente and Canesio D. Predo of the UPLB Institute of Renewable Natural Resources, College of Forestry and Natural Resources. It was published in the Philippine Journal of Science , Volume 154, No. 2, in April 2025. The researchers stressed that P75 is an estimated willingness to pay under a hypothetical scenario, not an existing fee or money currently being collected from resort visitors. Mt. Makiling is a dormant volcano and a vital watershed that supplies water for domestic, agricultural and industrial uses. Its hot springs and groundwater have also supported the growth of the resort industry in Calamba and Los Baños. READ: Fast Facts: Mt. Makiling Forest Reserve The study cited an earlier inventory that counted 1,043 resorts in the two areas as of 2020 — 871 in Calamba and 172 in Los Baños. The number of resorts in Calamba alone increased from 193 in 1998 to 466 in 2014, according to earlier research cited in the paper. “The growing number of resorts has naturally led to a surge in tourism,” the researchers wrote. The expansion of the resort industry has also meant greater use of groundwater. The researchers said many resorts had shifted from naturally flowing hot springs to pumping groundwater for their pools and other uses. They noted that resorts predominantly use pumped groundwater because it is cheaper than metered water from local water districts, which charge based on the volume consumed. The paper also cited an earlier survey that found resort pools had an average size of 80 cubic meters, with water temperatures ranging from above 30 C to 50 C. The researchers said drained pool water eventually reaches Laguna de Bay and pointed to the need to regulate and monitor its disposal. READ: The hot springs in Laguna may cool down soon Despite using resort pools supplied by groundwater or hot springs, many respondents were unsure about the source of the water. Of the 492 respondents, 52.6% said they knew the source of the resort’s water. Among those who identified a source, 26.2% said hot springs, 14.8% identified Mt. Makiling and only 7.3% identified groundwater. The researchers also found that 40.7% correctly identified pumping as the way pools were filled, while 34.1% believed the water flowed naturally. “A notable finding was that while 40.7% of respondents correctly identified pumping as the method for filling the pools, 34.1% mistakenly believed the water flowed naturally,” they wrote. The paper said this was significant because resorts in the area have increasingly relied on pumped groundwater rather than naturally flowing hot springs. Awareness was stronger when it came to the role of forests in maintaining groundwater. Some 98.4% of respondents agreed that good forest cover was important to securing groundwater supply, while 66.7% knew that groundwater was not unlimited. Still, 33% believed groundwater was unlimited regardless of how much water was used, the researchers found. The researchers described this as “disturbing,” noting that the findings “may imply a need to improve citizens’ understanding of water scarcity.” For most respondents, resort visits were primarily for recreation. The most common reason was relaxation or enjoyment, followed by the accessibility of resorts for family and friends and their affordability. “The main reasons of the respondents for visiting the resorts in Los Baños or Calamba are for relaxation (53%), to be with family and friends (39.6%), and because of the resorts’ accessibility (40%) and affordability (37.2%),” the researchers said. “About a fourth of the respondents went because they heard positive reviews either of a specific resort (28.3%) or the resorts in Los Baños and Calamba in general (27.4%) and for therapeutic or health reasons because of the perceived therapeutic properties of the hot water common in the pools (25%),” they added. PROTECTING MT. MAKILING’S GROUNDWATER Mt. Makiling’s forests and groundwater help sustain the resort industry in Calamba and Los Baños, Laguna. A University of the Philippines Los Baños study found that resort visitors were willing to pay an estimated P75 per visit for improved groundwater conservation, potentially generating P159.52 million a year if captured through a proposed water user fee. —PHOTO COURTESY OF MAKILING CENTER FOR MOUNTAIN ECOSYSTEMS The study also found that 81.7% of respondents were repeat visitors, having visited resorts in the area at least twice. Social media and recommendations from family and friends were among the main ways they learned about resorts. The researchers said the findings showed that the resort industry was not simply providing recreational services but was also drawing visitors who depended on the natural water resources associated with Mt. Makiling. The researchers used contingent valuation, a survey method that estimates how much people are willing to pay for an environmental resource or improvement that does not have a conventional market price. In the hypothetical scenario presented to respondents, local governments would require resorts to reuse and treat pool water rather than routinely replace it. An additional water user fee would be added to existing resort entrance fees. Under the proposed arrangement, half of the fee would be used to maintain pool water quality, while the other half would go toward the conservation of Mt. Makiling. Respondents were presented with payment amounts ranging from zero to more than P200 per visit. Of the 492 respondents, 488 selected an amount greater than zero. The most common choices were P50, selected by 25%, and P100, selected by 25.81%. Another 11.2% chose P20, while 8.1% selected P200. Only four respondents, or 0.81%, indicated zero willingness to pay. “The mean [willingness to pay] estimated using the payment card format was P75 [per] visit,” the researchers wrote. The P75 figure was calculated using interval regression based on the payment amounts selected by respondents. The researchers cautioned that the result represents stated preference rather than actual behavior or a guaranteed amount of revenue. “Stated preference techniques may be used when it is not possible to infer or observe people’s [willingness to pay] from markets or when markets are absent, as in the case of the groundwater resource of Mt. Makiling,” the study noted. The researchers found that the strongest motivation for willingness to pay was concern about Mt. Makiling’s groundwater. Among respondents who were willing to pay, 82.2% said they wanted to contribute to groundwater conservation on Mt. Makiling, while 52.3% cited the belief that groundwater is a finite resource. The researchers said only 28.2% cited the perception that current resort water use was wasteful as a reason for their willingness to pay. “Most respondents were willing to pay, primarily because they wanted to support the conservation of Mt. Makiling’s groundwater resources and recognized its limited availability,” the researchers wrote. READ: Makiling wildlife takes a breather The survey also found broad support for the conservation measures presented in the hypothetical scenario. About 84% agreed or completely agreed that conserving Mt. Makiling would enhance groundwater supply, while 78% agreed or completely agreed that recycling pool water would help conserve groundwater. About 75% agreed or completely agreed that the proposed groundwater conservation program was plausible. “For all three questions, there were more respondents who completely agreed than only agreed,” the researchers observed. The four respondents who indicated zero willingness to pay gave different reasons. Two did not believe groundwater was limited, one cited affordability, and another said visitors “should not be responsible for paying for pool water recycling.” The researchers said these responses showed that willingness to pay was influenced not only by environmental concerns but also by how visitors viewed the proposed fee and its affordability. To estimate how much could potentially be raised, the researchers multiplied the P75 mean willingness to pay by average annual resort visitor numbers in the two cities. For Calamba, they used an average of 2,015,124 resort visitors a year, based on visitor figures from 2013, 2014 and 2018. For Los Baños, they used an average of 111,821 visitors annually, based on available figures from 2013, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018 and 2019. This produced an estimated P151.13 million in annual potential revenue for Calamba and P8.39 million for Los Baños, or P159.52 million combined. The researchers estimated that, assuming the annual benefits remained constant, the amount would have a present value of P1.358 billion over 20 years at a 10% discount rate. “This present value can be used to decide policy options that will contribute to the conservation of Mt. Makiling’s groundwater resource,” the researchers said. Under the hypothetical fee arrangement used in the survey, half of the estimated annual revenue — or P79.76 million — could be allocated to improved management of Mt. Makiling, while the same amount could support water conservation practices among resorts. “These funds could support the enhanced management of Mt. Makiling and help resorts implement water conservation measures while maintaining pool water quality at international standards, reducing unnecessary and excessive water disposal,” the researchers stressed. The survey also asked respondents how often they believed resort pools should be emptied and refilled. Among visitors to public resorts, 45.5% believed pool water was changed daily, while 38.4% thought it was changed weekly. Among private-resort visitors, 42.5% believed water was changed daily and 19.3% thought it was changed every 12 hours. When asked how frequently water should ideally be replaced, 27% of public-resort visitors preferred replacement before every group’s use, while 39% preferred daily replacement. Among private-resort visitors, 46.5% preferred changing water before each group and 23% preferred daily replacement. The study also found a gap in visitors’ knowledge about pool water treatment. Only 23.4% knew that properly maintained and monitored pool water could remain in use for years without annual replacement, while 76.6% did not know this. At the same time, 67.9% said they would be less satisfied if they learned that pool water had not been changed for two years, even if it had been properly treated and maintained. “This points to the need for information dissemination about safe pool water standards,” the study noted. The study also examined factors associated with respondents’ willingness to pay. Its model found that age and water-conserving behavior were significant predictors. The researchers estimated that willingness to pay decreased by P0.802 for every additional year of age. Meanwhile, respondents who consistently practiced water conservation also had an estimated P27.23 lower willingness to pay than those who did not consistently practice water conservation. “Interestingly, respondents who do not consistently practice water conservation demonstrated a higher WTP. Conversely, those who already engage in water-conserving behaviors showed a lower WTP, possibly reflecting costs they have already absorbed for their current practices,” the researchers stated. The researchers recommended that local governments consider policies that would capture visitors’ stated willingness to pay and use the resulting funds for Mt. Makiling management and resort water conservation measures. The researchers also called for stronger information and education efforts among resort owners, visitors, the public, and local and national government officials to raise awareness of growing groundwater scarcity in Mt. Makiling and other parts of the country. “Additionally, resort owners should be informed about the importance of proper pool maintenance to minimize frequent and unnecessary water replacement,” the study noted. “In contrast, resort visitors should be educated on how pool water can meet international quality standards without excessive water use,” it added.

title: Groups press DENR to suspend mangrove earth-balling
author: Cristina Eloisa Baclig
environment_keywords: environment, environmental, sustainable, nature, natural resources, climate change, forest, conservation, ecosystem, ecosystems, ocean, marine, coastal, mangrove, mangroves, fisheries, flood, flooding, ecological
article_text: MANILA, Philippines — Environmental groups are urging the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to suspend the earth-balling and relocation of mangroves, warning that the practice could result in the death of up to 80% of trees removed, as a House resolution calls for an examination of the agency’s policy. The call was made by the Global Mangrove Alliance Philippines (GMAP), international ocean conservation organization Oceana and mangrove scientist Dr. Jurgenne Primavera of the Zoological Society of London (ZSL), amid a congressional inquiry into the DENR’s guidelines allowing mangrove earth-balling in exceptional circumstances. The DENR memorandum, dated Oct. 8, 2025, is titled Interim Operational Guidance and Conditions on the Earth-balling and Relocation of Mangroves in Exceptional Circumstances . It provides guidance for processing requests to earth-ball and relocate mangroves pending the completion of a study by the agency’s Ecosystems Research and Development Bureau. Under the memorandum, mangroves “shall not be removed or disturbed” as a rule. Earth-balling and relocation may be considered only in specified exceptional cases, including when mangrove trees pose a danger or when the activity involves an infrastructure flagship project endorsed by the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development, provided that mitigation measures to avoid impacts on mangroves have been exhausted. The guidelines also prohibit the DENR from accepting or processing requests for earth-balling and relocation for commercial, recreational or other private purposes. The environmental groups, however, said available scientific evidence raises concerns about whether mangroves removed through earth-balling can survive after transplantation. “Repeal the DENR Guidelines now. Congress must investigate to stop this threat to our remaining mangroves,” Primavera, ZSL’s chief mangroves scientific adviser, said. The groups cited several studies they said had been presented to the DENR as early as March 2025. These included a China-based study that recorded only 20% to 25% survival of two mangrove species 10 months after earth-balling; an Australia-based study that found mortality after 2.5 years among mangroves with an average trunk diameter of more than 5 centimeters; and Philippine data showing adult mangroves in five barangays in Ibajay, Aklan, had average trunk diameters of 9 to 16 centimeters. READ: Coastal greenbelt bill pushed as stronger storms threaten coasts The House resolution filed by Mamamayang Liberal Party-list Rep. Leila de Lima cites additional research indicating that successful earth-balling is ecologically and physiologically limited to trees with stem widths of less than approximately 8 centimeters. It also says mangroves in coastal areas typically targeted for infrastructure development in the Philippines have mature stems ranging from 10 to 30 centimeters in diameter or more. Earth-balling involves digging up a tree together with surrounding soil to form a compact mass, which is then secured and transferred using equipment such as a crane or bladed tree spade. “[S]tudies have shown that mangrove earth-balling and transplantation establish that the practice fundamentally disrupts the integrated soil-water-vegetation connections upon which mangrove ecosystems depend, resulting in losses of ecosystem function,” the House resolution stated. The DENR memorandum, meanwhile, states that the survival of earth-balled mangroves must be the “paramount consideration” in all cases. It requires proponents to follow established methodologies for selecting transplanting and replacement sites, preserving the root system and soil ball, timing the operation according to tidal and seasonal conditions, and using appropriate equipment and transport techniques. Proponents must also submit a Mangrove Rehabilitation and Monitoring Plan before any permit is issued. The memorandum further requires transplanting and replacement sites to meet ecological standards involving tidal elevation, hydrological conditions, salinity and soil conditions, slope and wave protection, and proximity to existing mangrove stands. For projects covered by the Philippine Environmental Impact Statement System, proposed earth-balling and relocation activities must also be included in the applicable environmental assessment documents. Actual earth-balling, transplanting and replacement planting must be conducted under the direct monitoring and supervision of the concerned DENR field office, according to the memorandum. Pending applications for mangrove earth-balling and relocation, meanwhile, will be evaluated under the safeguards in the memorandum. “Proponents with incomplete requirements or pending submissions shall be directed to update their applications in compliance with these provisions prior to further evaluation. No permit shall be issued unless full compliance with this Memorandum is observed,” the agency said. The memorandum also says existing guidelines and requirements for the issuance of cutting or earth-balling permits will remain in effect and will apply alongside the new provisions. It also provides that unauthorized cutting, earth-balling or relocation of mangroves may be subject to penalties under Presidential Decree No. 705, as amended, the Fisheries Code and other applicable laws. Beyond the scientific concerns, the House resolution questions whether the DENR memorandum is consistent with existing laws and international commitments on mangrove protection. It cites Section 99 of Republic Act No. 8550, as amended by RA 10654, or the Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998, which prohibits the conversion of mangroves for other purposes. The resolution also points to Presidential Proclamation No. 2152, which declares the entire province of Palawan and certain other areas as mangrove swamp forest reserves, and the Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Act, or RA 8371, when mangrove areas fall within ancestral domains. The resolution argues that the DENR’s issuance could conflict with these protections, describing the “unilateral issuance of administrative guidance” as a “grave overreach of executive regulatory authority.” READ: Mangroves save lives: Greenbelt zones pushed in PH It also asks House committees to examine the memorandum’s legal validity and determine whether it should be revoked or amended. Specifically, the resolution calls for the inquiry to “review the legal validity of the administrative issuance in light of existing mangrove protection laws, recommend its immediate revocation or amendment as may be warranted, and call for the conduct of a comprehensive, independent scientific review.” The proposed inquiry would also look beyond the current memorandum. De Lima’s resolution asks lawmakers to review and consolidate existing legislation and explore a new mangrove conservation and protection law establishing “clear, enforceable standards for mangrove preservation, rehabilitation, and sustainable management.” The Philippines is home to at least 50% of the roughly 65 mangrove species found worldwide, but its mangrove cover has declined from about 500,000 hectares in the early 20th century to roughly 285,000 to 311,400 hectares in 2020, according to Oceana. The House resolution puts the remaining cover at about 284,798 hectares and says the country has lost more than 64% of its mangroves since 1918. READ: DPWH flood project in Cebu buries mangroves without environmental permit The resolution notes that mangroves help protect coastal communities from storm surges, flooding and erosion while also serving as nurseries for marine species, supporting fisherfolk livelihoods and contributing to climate change mitigation. For Oceana Vice President Von Hernandez, allowing earth-balling could put those natural defenses at further risk. “By allowing earth-balling, the DENR is sacrificing proven nature-based solutions for short-term economic gain,” Hernandez said. “Shouldn’t the DENR be held accountable for reneging on its mandate to protect mangroves and uphold nature-based safeguards especially at a time when every coastal community in the country is under siege from flooding and storm surges?” he added. Oceana also pointed to Cancabato Bay in Tacloban City, Leyte — known as “ground zero” of Supertyphoon Yolanda (Haiyan) in 2013, one of the deadliest typhoons in recorded history, which killed at least 6,300 people — as a potential site for further mangrove removal. The organization said operators of Daniel Z. Romualdez Airport announced on July 29 that “mangroves in the airport’s vicinity will have to be removed to make way for shore protection infrastructure, a new perimeter road, and to prevent bird strikes.” According to GMAP, many coastal areas with mangroves targeted for cutting were declared no-build zones after Supertyphoon Haiyan. GMAP has called for a halt to earth-balling while Congress examines the policy. “In the spirit of precaution, all earth-balling of mangroves must stop while Congress examines the scientific, legal, and governance questions surrounding the policy,” the group said. The groups also cited the 40-hectare Floodway Project in Jaro, Iloilo, as an example of infrastructure being integrated into a natural mangrove environment. They are urging the passage of the proposed National Coastal Greenbelt Bill, which seeks to strengthen mangrove restoration and nature-based solutions for vulnerable coastal communities. Oceana said it supports De Lima’s investigation and the proposed legislation. By providing an email address. title: PH climate-health research heavily focused on Luzon – study
author: Cristina Eloisa Baclig
environment_keywords: climate change, climate crisis, climate mitigation, extreme weather, el niño, la niña, greenhouse gas, decarbonization, conservation, ecosystem, air quality, particulate matter, water conservation, flood, flooding, drought, ecological, ecology
article_text: MANILA, Philippines — The weeks of heavy rainfall that caused flooding in parts of the Philippines have again brought the health risks associated with extreme weather into public view. But while research on climate change and health in the country has increased in recent years, a University of the Philippines (UP)-led review found that much of the research remains concentrated in Luzon, with relatively few studies using long-term climate and health data. The findings came from a review of 69 studies on climate change and health in the Philippines published between 2018 and 2023. Published in Frontiers in Climate in July 2025, the study was conducted by researchers from the UP-National Institutes of Health and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit. The researchers found a substantial increase in climate-health research compared with an earlier review covering 1980 to 2017, including notable growth in studies on mental health, gender-based vulnerabilities and adaptation measures. However, important gaps remained. “[R]esearch remains geographically concentrated in Luzon,” the researchers wrote, noting that “few studies utilized long-term climate-health datasets.” Studies measuring the health co-benefits of climate mitigation also remained limited. The review was led by Clarissa De Guzman, Megan Lorenza Cabaero, Jude Raphael Lo, Jimmy Loro, Maria Vinna Crisostomo, Michelle Ylade and Kristal An Agrupis. The researchers screened 8,436 scientific articles from various databases before identifying 69 studies that met their criteria for inclusion. The studies were grouped into six areas: vulnerability to disease and injury; direct health effects of climate and weather; ecosystem-mediated health impacts; health impacts mediated through human institutions; adaptation strategies; and the health co-benefits of climate mitigation. Of the 69 studies, 54 used quantitative research methods. Twenty-seven were ecological studies, and 20 were cross-sectional studies. Eleven studies examined mosquito-borne diseases, 10 focused on psychological outcomes, nine examined air quality-related health outcomes, and another nine looked at temperature-related health outcomes. READ: UP study finds storm patterns in PH that can guide response Research output also increased toward the end of the study period, with 16 studies published in 2022 and another 16 in 2023. The researchers compared these findings with an earlier scoping review that examined Philippine research from 1980 to 2017 and identified 40 articles over 37 years. The new review found 69 studies over six years, representing a 72.5% increase in the number of studies identified. The researchers said the increase, particularly in 2022 and 2023, suggested growing recognition of climate change as a public health issue. The increase was also reflected in the range of health issues being studied. Research examining health impacts mediated through human institutions grew from one study in the earlier review to 26 studies, or 37.7%, in the latest review. These covered areas such as mental health, gender-based violence and occupational stress. The researchers said the increase in studies examining mental, psychological and psychosocial health may reflect growing policy attention to mental health in the Philippines. They pointed to the inclusion of mental health in the 2017-2022 National Unified Health Research Agenda, the enactment of the Philippine Mental Health Act in 2018 and the development of the country’s first National Mental Health Research Agenda in 2019. “Examining the various health impacts of climate change beyond disease, injury, and mortality offers a more comprehensive understanding of its broad effects on public health and paves the way for more integrative solutions,” the researchers wrote. Despite the increase in publications, the studies were not evenly distributed geographically. “Geographically, most studies were concentrated in Luzon, particularly in the National Capital Region (NCR),” the researchers wrote. At the barangay, city, provincial or regional level, 13 studies were conducted in Luzon, compared with 10 in Mindanao and seven in the Visayas. While fewer studies were conducted in the Visayas and Mindanao, those studies were more spread out across the two island groups than those in Luzon. The researchers said the imbalance may be related to differences in research funding and institutional capacity. Funding data showed that 39 of the 69 studies were funded by foreign institutions. Five received funding from both foreign and Philippine-based institutions, while only six were funded solely by Philippine-based institutions. Nineteen studies did not report a funding source. The researchers said the predominance of foreign-funded studies further highlighted the need for greater domestic investment in climate-health research capacity. The geographic concentration also matters because climate-related health risks can differ depending on location, exposure and local capacity to respond. One study cited in the review found that Manila City had very high heat-health risk, while other cities in NCR were also among those with the highest heat-health risks. At the same time, some of the most heat-vulnerable cities were outside the capital, where coping capacity was lower. Other research examined differences in tropical cyclone exposure and mortality across regions, including higher cyclone risks in parts of the Visayas and southern Luzon and substantial typhoon-related mortality in the Visayas. The geographic gap was not the only weakness identified by the researchers. The review also found that very few studies used sufficiently long climate-health datasets to examine trends over extended periods. The researchers noted that the World Meteorological Organization recommends a 30-year period for determining average climate conditions. Such a period allows researchers to account for year-to-year variations and anomalies, including El Niño and La Niña, while identifying longer-term trends. Only nine of the 69 studies met that 30-year threshold. All nine, however, relied on international data sources. “To our knowledge, no long-term study of at least 30 years using exclusively local climate and health data from the Philippines currently exists,” the researchers wrote. The researchers said the absence of long-term studies using local data may be partly related to problems involving the availability and consistency of climate and health records. They also cautioned that shorter studies may fail to capture longer-term trends and could lead to premature conclusions about the relationship between climate variables and disease. The researchers recommended longer surveillance periods that combine local meteorological information with health outcomes, including studies that can attribute mortality and illness to extreme heat, floods and typhoons. They also called for prospective cohort studies, which follow groups of people over time, to provide a better understanding of the longer-term effects of climate change on health. The 69 studies covered a broad range of climate-related health risks. The largest group, comprising 36 studies, or 52.2%, examined ecosystem-mediated impacts, including vector-borne and parasitic diseases, infectious diseases, noncommunicable diseases, and air and water quality. Another 26 studies, or 37.7%, examined health impacts mediated through human institutions, including mental and psychosocial health, violence and conflict, occupational health and nutrition. Nineteen studies focused on vulnerability to disease and injury, 16 examined direct impacts of climate and weather, and 14 looked at adaptation strategies. Only five studies, or 7.2%, examined the health co-benefits of climate mitigation. Nine studies focused on heat-related health impacts. The review cited research estimating that for every 1-degree Celsius increase in temperature, excess mortality in the Philippines could rise by 32.7%. Other studies linked high temperatures to diarrhea, hospitalizations and deaths, cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease. Children and older adults were among the groups identified as particularly vulnerable. Among children younger than 5, high ambient temperatures were associated with enteric infections. At San Lazaro Hospital in Manila, more than half of hospitalizations and deaths from severe diarrhea associated with high temperatures occurred among children in this age group. A study of typhoon mortality from 2005 to 2015 found that people 60 and older had the highest mortality count per 100,000. READ: Elderly far more at risk from rising heat than thought – study The review also cited research showing that children exposed to disasters faced increased risks of mortality, injuries, illness, violence and malnutrition. Typhoons and floods were likewise associated with deaths, injuries and infectious diseases. Following Typhoon Yolanda, a field hospital in Ormoc City reported acute respiratory infections, acute watery diarrhea and skin diseases among children ages 0 to 4. READ: Climate change, no longer a distant threat, is hurting kids now The relationship between climate and health can also vary according to local conditions. “Climate, topography, and socioeconomic factors are critical in determining temperature mortality rates, particularly in the tropics like the Philippines, where the mortality risk rises significantly above 35.6°C,” the researchers wrote. Several studies examined relationships between climate variables and mosquito-borne diseases, particularly dengue. Rainfall, temperature and humidity were among the factors associated with dengue incidence, although the relationship varied depending on location and the climate variable examined. YOUNG VICTIMS Dengue-stricken children share a bed in a hospital in Quezon City. —Marianne Bermudez A nationwide study found that dengue risk increased with average temperature up to 27.5°C before declining. Other studies, however, produced different results in specific locations. READ: Fifth of dengue cases due to climate change – researchers The review also cited evidence connecting heavy rainfall and flooding with leptospirosis. In Manila, heavy rainfall was associated with increased leptospirosis hospitalizations linked to flooding. Other studies connected precipitation with risks from emerging infectious diseases. READ: Manila warns of flu, dengue, leptospirosis risks amid rainy season Following Typhoon Yolanda, communicable diseases accounted for 88.2% of medical consultations in Ormoc City, with acute respiratory infections accounting for 73.1%. Patients pack the gymnasium of the National Kidney Institute (NKTI) in Quezon City of chronic bronchitis patients and leptospirosis cases on August 11, 2025. —Inquirer photo/Grig C. Montegrande The researchers also noted that climate-related health risks are shaped by differences in vulnerability and capacity across communities. “Provinces with high population density and poverty incidence had higher dengue risks at upper-temperature ranges,” the researchers explained. One of the clearest areas of growth was research into mental, psychological and psychosocial health. Eighteen of the 26 studies examining health impacts mediated through human institutions focused on mental health and related outcomes. The studies covered climate anxiety, trauma, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety and other psychological effects associated with extreme weather events. One study involving 10,000 young people ages 16 to 25 found that 75% viewed the future as frightening. Other research cited in the review linked climate-related emotions such as fear, sadness, anxiety, guilt and worry with insomnia and poorer self-assessed mental health. READ: PH among world’s most water-stressed countries due to climate change Women in the Philippines reported greater climate-related emotional distress than men in one study, including higher levels of worry and stronger feelings of betrayal by governments. Disaster survivors reported anxiety, panic, isolation and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), while social networks were identified as a potential source of psychosocial resilience. READ: ‘Eco-anxiety’: PH children among most stressed by climate crisis The researchers said more longitudinal studies and context-specific psychosocial support models were needed, particularly after disasters. “Additional research should also examine how institutional responses (e.g., education systems, labor conditions, food security programs) mediate health outcomes during and after climate shocks,” the researchers said. The studies reviewed by the researchers showed that climate-related health impacts can overlap with existing social and economic vulnerabilities. Research following Typhoons Yolanda and Sendong documented conflicts, displacement and difficulties in evacuation and resettlement. Other studies found increases in gender-based violence, including domestic violence, sexual abuse and human trafficking after disasters. Occupational health was another concern. In Angat, Bulacan, 39.19% of household farmers surveyed reported significant health impacts associated with drought, including hypertension, dehydration and diarrhea. DEVASTATION Residents of Tacloban City sift through debris after Supertyphoon “Yolanda” hit Leyte province in November 2013. —RICHARD REYES Transport workers in flood-prone parts of Bulacan and Malabon also faced work disruptions and safety concerns during flooding. Health care workers were affected as well. Flooding disrupted clinical shifts, contributed to staff shortages and increased fatigue. One study cited in the review found PTSD symptoms among 30% of first-line medical responders, while 7% experienced depression. READ: MENTAL HEALTH ABSENT IN PH CLIMATE CHANGE PLANS Food security was also affected. The review cited research showing that children exposed to natural disasters were more likely to experience severe food insecurity and stunting. FEEDING TIME A malnourished child eats rice porridge and adobo at a feeding session held in Baseco, Tondo, Manila. According to Unicef, malnutrition is partly driven by the increasing availability of processed food, especially to poor families. —INQUIRER FILE PHOTO National Nutrition Survey data cited by one study showed that 37.8% of households had experienced typhoons and 24.3% had experienced floods, affecting their ability to meet recommended energy intake. Among children of fishermen in Davao, average daily energy intake was lower during summer than during the northeast monsoon and remained below the Philippine Dietary Reference Intakes during both periods. Fourteen of the 69 studies examined adaptation strategies designed to protect health. At the individual level, one study found that 94.8% of surveyed Filipinos took steps to prepare for an incoming disaster. These included monitoring television, radio and social media, preparing food, water and medicine, securing important documents and belongings, and following evacuation procedures. At the community level, studies documented measures such as elevating roads, installing floodgates, dredging waterways and conducting disaster drills. The review also documented Indigenous and community-based practices, including water conservation, maintaining water facilities, clearing drainage canals and selecting climate-resilient crops. READ: Harvard study shows Filipinos better prepared for disasters Members of the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) team prepare rescue equipment at their headquarters in Pasig City on Wednesday, July 8, as Super Typhoon #IndayPH enters the Philippine Area of Responsibility. —Grig C. Montegrande, Philippine Daily Inquirer However, access to adaptation and health care resources remained uneven. Some disaster survivors faced long distances to health facilities, transportation difficulties, shortages of medicines and doctors, language barriers and financial constraints that limited access to care. The researchers said future work should assess whether adaptation measures actually work rather than simply document whether communities use them. “[F]uture research should evaluate the effectiveness of individual and community-level responses, including the use of traditional knowledge, disaster kits, health-seeking behaviors, and early warning systems,” they wrote. They also recommended working with local governments and communities at risk to develop and validate adaptation tools and metrics. The smallest category in the review involved the health co-benefits of climate mitigation. Only five of the 69 studies examined this area, including the potential health effects of lower greenhouse gas emissions, cleaner transportation and improved air quality. The review cited modeling studies showing that lower-emission pathways could reduce heat-related mortality, while reducing vehicle emissions could improve air quality and lower risks associated with cancer, cardiovascular disease and respiratory illnesses. READ: SWS: 87% of Filipinos experienced effects of climate change One study estimated that reducing nitrogen dioxide under a decarbonization scenario could prevent 3,601 childhood asthma cases in a year. Another estimated that reducing particulate matter could prevent 852 cases of preterm birth and 896 cases of low birth weight per 100,000 preterm deliveries. The researchers said more studies were needed to quantify these health benefits and their economic value. “There is a critical need to quantify the health and economic returns of emissions reduction strategies,” they wrote, citing clean-energy transitions, improved air quality and reduced vehicle emissions as areas for further research. The review identified several priorities for strengthening climate-health research in the Philippines. One is longer-term, locally generated data. The researchers recommended long-term, high-resolution climate-health surveillance using local meteorological and health data, including studies that can attribute specific illnesses and deaths to extreme heat, floods and typhoons. Another priority is more localized research. Only 11 of the 69 studies, or 15.9%, were conducted at the city level. The researchers said city-level studies could help local governments identify climate-health trends specific to their communities and develop more targeted interventions. They also called for stronger national research databases. Only four studies in the review were sourced from the country’s two main health research databases, the Health Research and Development Information Network and the Philippine Health Research Registry. PARCHED | In this photo taken in May 2023, a boy walks through a parched rice field in Tanza, Cavite, as the state weather bureau issued an El Niño alert. —Marianne Bermudez, Philippine Daily Inquirer The researchers recommended improving the accessibility, indexing and search functions of these platforms to reduce duplication and improve coordination of climate-health research. More studies should also examine how climate-related vulnerabilities differ by age, gender, geography, socioeconomic status and displacement. “Disaggregated data and population-specific analyses are essential to inform targeted interventions,” the researchers wrote, particularly for children, older adults and migrants. For ecosystem-related health risks, the authors also recommended complementing human health research with entomological studies examining how climate affects vector ecology and disease transmission. The researchers cautioned that the review had several limitations. They did not conduct a formal quality or risk-of-bias assessment because the study aimed to map research trends and gaps rather than establish cause-and-effect relationships. The review also excluded entomological studies, which meant some research on how climate affects disease vectors was not captured. Because the review relied on published, peer-reviewed studies, unpublished, ongoing and some community-based research may likewise have been missed. Still, the researchers said the gaps identified in the review point to the need for more localized and longer-term climate-health research. “Local studies will help inform local government units on climate-health trends specific to their area, enabling more targeted interventions,” they wrote. /dm

title: Analyst: ‘Sea of garbage’ reflects PH’s poor environmental standing
author: Kurt Dela Peña
asean_countries: Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam
environment_keywords: environmental, waste, garbage, solid waste, waste management, flood, ecological
article_text: MANILA, Philippines — As waste generation strains collection, segregation and disposal systems, rivers and canals across Metro Manila have become disposal areas. This is why the “sea of garbage” exposed by receding floodwaters last week was not surprising, data scientist Dr. Alicor Panao said. “No less than the President described the garbage situation as ‘critical,’ warning that waste entering waterways was clogging flood-control infrastructure,” he said. Panao, an associate professor at the University of the Philippines, said that while the images were shocking, they should not have come as a surprise. READ: Parañaque gov’t starts clearing trash from Baclaran waterway He pointed out that the Philippines ranked 162nd among 177 countries in the Environmental Performance Index (EPI), with a score of 27.87. “That is 8.97 points below the Asia-Pacific average of 36.84,” he said. In the Asia-Pacific region, the Philippines ranked 21st among 24 countries, ahead only of Indonesia, Vietnam and Laos, which scored 26.24, 23.82 and 21.78, respectively. Panao said this showed that the country was trailing several of its regional neighbors in Southeast Asia. READ: Over 200 truckloads of garbage hauled from Parañaque water channel Based on the EPI, Singapore had a score of 46.06; Thailand, 43.74; Malaysia, 39.52; Cambodia, 31.21; and Myanmar, 28.87. “The Philippines’ environmental performance has worsened over the 10-year period, at least as measured by the EPI,” he said. Over the past decade, the country’s score fell by 1.35 points, while Malaysia’s improved by 8.47 points, Thailand’s by 7.31 and China’s by 10.10. For Panao, this “reflects problems that extend beyond the garbage unraveled by storms,” as 70% of Metro Manila’s drainage systems are reportedly clogged with garbage and silt. He said heavy reliance on single-use plastics, weak segregation at source and illegal dumping also allow waste to move from streets into waterways. Panao said reversing the trend requires prevention rather than repeated post-flood cleanup. “The Philippines does not lack solutions. What it has lacked is the political will and institutional capacity to implement them,” he said. Panao said the government should strictly enforce all requirements laid out in Republic Act No. 9003, or the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, including segregation at source, proper collection and disposal, and functioning materials recovery facilities at the barangay level.
